extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, litigators, and law students (those drafting or construing patent specifications and claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to prepare and construe patent specifications and claims so they satisfy statutory requirements (enablement, disclosure) and proper claim scope (combination vs principle, device vs process). Useful for drafters and those litigating claim scope and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent for application of a principle (generality of claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may claim the application of a newly discovered principle to a specified result; the patent may cover the mode of carrying that principle into effect rather than a single specific form of apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Minter v. Wells (self-adjusting chair): claiming a self-adjusting lever applied to the back of a chair — held to cover any chair constructed on that principle. Neilson (hot blast): patent construed as for the application of blowing with hot air by means of a vessel heating the air between blowing apparatus and furnace; the 'shape of the receptacle is immaterial' and the patent embraced all forms of apparatus effecting the same principle. The generality of claiming 'all modes of applying the principle to the purpose specified' is not in itself an objection; breadth may be the merit of the invention where the patentee has disclosed the principle and a mode of applying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming a mode of carrying a principle into effect (broad claim when no particular form is essential)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor suggests the principle and also invents how it may be applied to a practical result by mechanical contrivance, and shows awareness that no particular form of apparatus is essential, he may claim the mode of carrying the principle into effect without confining himself to one form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court rationale: requiring a patentee to confine to one form would often prevent patents for valuable discoveries because the best form cannot be known at once. If any sort of apparatus applied in the stated way will produce the benefit, the patentee need not be tied to a specific form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of material matter in specification (fraudulent concealment vs degree-of-benefit omissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must not voluntarily conceal anything material to the invention or add anything unnecessary for the purpose of deceiving the public; omission of something necessary for beneficial enjoyment is fatal, but omission of something that only affects the degree of benefit is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory defense: specification that 'does not contain the whole truth relative to his invention... or contains more than is necessary... which concealment or addition shall fully appear to have been made for the purpose of deceiving the public.' Fraudulent concealment or adding useless matter—if done to deceive—voids the patent. However, leaving out details that only influence the degree (not the practice) of the invention is not fatal (illustrated in Neilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether patent claims a combination or distinct inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must decide whether the patentee claims a combination of several things or distinct inventions of several things; if one or more elements are not new, the question becomes whether the patent can be sustained for the combination as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: a patent for a combination of three things cannot at the same time be a patent for a combination of any two of them; if the subject-matter is the combination of a given number of parts, no portion less than the whole is, simultaneously, the subject-matter. Example: agricultural machine claims covering multiple interconnected parts — using a single part (knife) alone was held not to infringe because patent was for the combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must not be mere claims for a result (no result-only claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely states a desired result without claiming the means or construction to achieve it is bad; claims should be to the construction or arrangement 'in substantially the manner described.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coffin v. Ogden: first claim phrased as a result was held bad; the valid construction is a claim to dividing the hub or follower 'in substantially the manner described' and combining it with the reversible latch as described. Always tie the claimed result to the structural/operational features disclosed in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims and specification must be read together (interpretation in light of description and drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be interpreted in the light of the specification and drawings; the whole claim, read with the specification, should disclose the organized mechanism which the inventor has patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Shipman's instruction in Blake v. Stafford: alleged vagueness can be resolved by reading claims alongside the detailed description and drawings. The specification + drawings may plainly disclose the mechanism and cure objections of vagueness when considered together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: device vs process (claim language controls what is claimed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must construe claims to determine whether they are for a process or for a device/instrument; the same wording may be interpreted as a device when the claim describes an instrument to be employed in a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Railroad Co. v. Dubois: claim for 'building and setting piers by means of a floating coffer-dam, substantially as set forth' was construed as a claim to a device (floating coffer-dam) rather than to a process, and the court refused to require proof of use of a particular process. Drafters should be mindful of wording ('the use of the tube...','in combination with') and the court's likely construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing statutory categories or incompatible claim types
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent should not contain claims that fall under different statutory regimes or that are essentially distinct types of subject-matter (e.g., a machine and a design protected under different acts) in a way that renders the patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clark v. Bousfield: the second claim was argued to be merely a design; court held the elastic bed in the machine (even if embodying designs) constituted an element of the machine and thus was within the machine patent. Nevertheless, drafters must avoid claims that improperly mix categories (which may have different protection terms) unless the specification clearly makes them part of the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of claim language will be interpreted in ordinary use
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad terms in claims (e.g., 'iron frame') may be read to encompass whatever, in ordinary language, would be called by that term, not necessarily limited to a particular embodiment described elsewhere in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: English case where 'iron frame' in a broad claim was held to include any iron frame that would ordinarily be called such, not only the specific frame in another claim. Be cautious: breadth invites scrutiny for prior art that may anticipate the broad claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read description before construing claims (claims not in isolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper approach is to read the inventor's description of the invention first so the drafter/reader is prepared for what the inventor then claims; claims should not be divorced from the preceding detailed description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Hatherly in Arnold v. Bradbury: read the description first to understand what is claimed; claims that appear broad may be limited in meaning by the specification's detail. Also, inventor may reserve right to make modifications 'substantially the same' as present invention — court will respect that if the description shows such intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable a person skilled in the art to practise the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding the invention 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity' as to enable any person skilled in the art to make, construct, compound, and use the invention from the specification alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute requires explaining the principle and the several modes contemplated for application and to 'particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination' claimed. Whether the specification suffices is a question of fact for a jury; technical terms are permissible but may need explanatory evidence. The specification need not teach a layperson — it must enable a person of competent skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity judged from viewpoint of skilled artisan (not layperson)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether the specification is ambiguous or uncertain, the relevant standard is whether persons skilled in the particular art would find it ambiguous, not whether the layperson would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute allows addressing the description to persons of competent skill; thus specifications may employ technical terms that require expert explanation. Distinguish ambiguity to the general public from ambiguity to skilled artisans when evaluating sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims limited to what is novel and described (prior art limits scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where a patentee describes and claims broadly, if subsequent evidence shows that the claim 'takes in that which has already been invented' (prior art), the claim may fail — breadth cannot capture what is not novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Hatherly's observation: a broad claim might be invalid not because it claims too much in form, but because it covers subject-matter already invented. Drafters should ensure novelty of what is claimed and be prepared that broad language invites challenge by prior art.
